studies.title: The Home Of Peace
studies.meaning: Two motions are described and they are not the same. God calls to the Home of Peace, and He guides whom He wills to a straight path, so an open invitation and a particular guiding stand together in one sentence. The commentators keep both without dissolving the tension. Then the reward: goodness, and something extra which is left unnamed. The explanation most often given for the addition is the sight of God, though the ayah says only more.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah largely occupied with people who wanted a different kind of sign and who treated this life as the whole account. The passage arrives just after a parable comparing worldly life to vegetation that flourishes and is cut down overnight. The commentators read the invitation as the answer to that parable, and record no specific occasion for the ayat themselves.

keyTerms.note: The word for a dwelling with a courtyard, a household rather than a building. Joined to a word for wholeness and safety, it names the destination as a place to live in rather than a state to reach.
A plain word for addition, left without an object. The commentators most often explain it as the sight of God, and note that the ayah deliberately leaves the extra unspecified.
A film of dust or smoke settling on something, the darkening that comes over a face at bad news. Denying it is a physical description, since the face is where humiliation shows first.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Faces were read constantly in that society. A man returning from a failed negotiation, a family that had lost a claim, a debtor passing his creditor: everyone knew the news before anybody spoke. Poetry describes the dust of humiliation settling on a man's features. Promising that neither dust nor lowliness would touch these faces spoke to a culture where standing was worn openly.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the phrase Home of Peace only twice, here and at 6:127, and in both places it is paired with a statement about God's relation to those who receive it. The word for peace inside it is the same one used as the greeting exchanged there, so the destination is named after what is said inside it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The invitation is universal and the guidance is particular, and the passage sets them side by side without softening either. Classical discussion has kept both, treating the call as genuinely addressed to everyone while the arrival is not in human hands alone. The reward then refuses to be measured: goodness is matched to what was done, and something further is added with no stated equivalent.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same name for the destination, adding that He is their ally.
Precedes it with the parable of vegetation cut down that this invitation answers.
States the principle of matching, that the reward of good is nothing but good.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often the word peace passes your lips today as a greeting, and let one of those be deliberate. The destination in this ayah is named after that word. It costs nothing to mean it once, and the passage suggests the greeting and the address are the same thing at different distances.

studies.title: Healing For What Is Inside
studies.meaning: Four things are named and the address narrows as it goes. Counsel arrives for all people, then healing for what is in the chests, then guidance and mercy, and these last two are specified for believers. The commentators note that healing is placed before guidance, so the text is described as treating something before it teaches anything. The following ayah then tells people what to be glad about, and weighs it against what they accumulate.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is largely addressed to an audience arguing about where the revelation came from, and this passage steps outside that argument to describe what the text does instead. The commentators record no specific occasion, and read the address to all people as a deliberate widening after a long stretch aimed at opponents.

keyTerms.note: Speech aimed at softening rather than informing, the kind that works on the will. Naming it first places the text's effect before its content, which the sequence of the ayah then continues.
The ordinary medical word for recovery from illness. Its object here is what is in the chests, so the trouble being treated is located inside a person rather than in their circumstances.
The Quran uses this for the seat of what a person conceals: doubt, resentment, intention. Naming the chest rather than the heart points at the container rather than at the organ inside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medicine in Arabia was practical and limited: cautery, cupping, honey, herbs, and the setting of bones. Illnesses of the chest were understood physically, and the vocabulary of cure was familiar to everyone. Using that word for what a recitation does to a person's inner state borrowed language from a craft the audience trusted, and applied it to something nobody could see.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes itself as healing in several places, and the descriptions always carry a limit. One passage calls it healing and mercy for believers while adding nothing but loss for wrongdoers; another calls it guidance and healing for those who believe and something quite different for those who do not.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as treatment before instruction, which assumes a particular diagnosis: the obstacle to guidance is not a lack of information but something lodged inside a person. That explains how the same text can be read by two people with opposite results. The following ayah then relocates joy, moving it from what has been gathered to what has been given, and it does so by command rather than by argument.

crossReferences.why: Calls the revelation healing and mercy for believers, and loss for wrongdoers.
Describes it as guidance and healing for some and as deafness for others.
Names the remembrance of God as what settles hearts, describing the same effect.

studies.applyIt: Pick one passage you find difficult, and instead of asking what it teaches, ask what it disturbs. Sit with the discomfort for a minute rather than resolving it. The ayah puts healing before guidance, and treatment usually feels worse than instruction before it starts feeling better.

studies.title: The Friends Of God
studies.meaning: An attention marker opens the passage, the particle used to announce something. Then a claim about the allies of God, followed by a definition that is deliberately plain: those who believed and used to guard themselves. No rank, no title, no separate class. Good news is promised in this life as well as the next, and the words are said to be unalterable. The last ayah turns to the messenger and tells him not to be saddened by talk.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah addressing people who claimed intermediaries and privileged access. The definition given here is read by the commentators as answering that: the category of God's allies is fixed by two ordinary qualities available to anybody. Classical sources record several explanations of the good news promised in this life, including true dreams, and preserve the range without settling it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for nearness and for taking charge of someone. The word describes a two-sided closeness, which is why the same term is used of God towards believers elsewhere in the Quran.
From a root for skin and for the face brightening at news. The word names the physical effect of good news, so what is promised includes something felt rather than only something learned.
Strength that cannot be reached or reduced, the quality that made a fortified place impregnable. Saying that all of it belongs to God removes the standing the speakers were relying on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Holy men in Arabia held a recognised social role. Diviners, keepers of shrines and men credited with contact with the unseen were consulted, paid, and treated as a class apart. A definition of God's friends that named only belief and self-restraint, with no rite, lineage or shrine attached, cut across an established profession and the fees that came with it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase promising no fear and no grief recurs through the Quran, always in the same shape, and here it is attached not to a named community but to a category defined in the ayah that follows. Classical commentators treat the two ayat as a single sentence for that reason, since the claim would otherwise be left without a subject.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Closeness to God is described as available rather than allocated, and the definition given is short enough to check yourself against. The good news promised in this life keeps the passage from being wholly postponed, without specifying what it consists of, which the commentators leave open. The instruction at the end then reframes opposition: what people say is answered by a statement about where power sits.

crossReferences.why: Names God as the ally of those who believe, the other side of the word used here.
Describes angels descending on those who stayed upright with the same reassurance.
States that all honour belongs to God, answering those who seek it elsewhere.

studies.applyIt: Check yourself against the definition rather than against an ideal. Two things are named, believing and guarding yourself, and neither requires a title. If the phrase friends of God has always sounded to you like a description of somebody else, notice that the passage spends its next line making sure it is not.

studies.title: Nothing Can Turn It Back
studies.meaning: The two halves are not built the same way, and the difference is the point. Harm is described as a touch, with its removal denied to anyone but Him. Good is described as something He intends for you, with nothing able to turn His bounty back. The second clause moves from contact to purpose, and the commentators note that the asymmetry runs in favour of the good. The closing names are forgiveness and mercy rather than power.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing passage of a surah that has spent its length on people calling upon things that could neither harm nor help them. The ayat before it gather the whole argument into an instruction about which way to turn. This is the final piece of that summary, and the commentators read the two divine names at the end as the surah's chosen resting point.

keyTerms.note: An agent noun from the verb to send something back. It pictures bounty as already in motion, so refusing it would mean intercepting something on its way rather than preventing a decision.

keyTerms.gloss: intends for you, wants for you
keyTerms.note: A verb of will rather than of contact. Set opposite the word for touching in the first half, it gives the good a source in intention while the harm is described only as arriving.
A general word for damage of any kind. Its indefinite form leaves the scale unspecified, so the sentence covers a minor setback and a catastrophe in exactly the same terms.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Intercession with the powerful was how anything got done. A man in trouble found someone with standing to speak for him, and a favour granted could be blocked by a rival with better access. Everyone understood that gifts could be intercepted on the way. Saying that nothing turns back this bounty described a channel with nobody standing in it, which was a strange idea in a world of brokers.
studies.didYouKnow: The first half of this ayah appears almost word for word earlier in the Quran, at 6:17, but the second half differs. There the good is a touch, matching the harm; here it is something intended, and the closing divine names change along with it. The variation is small enough to vanish in translation and consistent in the Arabic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established at once, and they pull in different directions unless read carefully. Nothing reaches a person outside God's decree, and nothing can obstruct what He intends for them. The first removes the illusion of independent threats; the second removes the fear of blocked good. Ending on forgiveness and mercy rather than on might tells the reader which of the two the passage expects them to need.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same statement with its second half built differently, in a Meccan surah.
States that whatever mercy God opens for people, nobody can withhold it.
Asks whether the things called upon beside God could hold back His mercy.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good thing you have stopped hoping for because of who is standing in the way: a person, a system, a decision that went against you. Say the second half of this ayah about that specific case. You are not predicting an outcome. You are checking whether you had quietly promoted an obstacle into a decider.
